questions.explanation: With one argument, slice returns everything from that index to the end, dropping the first character of '294'. The result is '94'. The printed value is 94, while the alternatives come from assuming slice copies the whole string, keeping the removed first character and stopping after one character.
questions.hint: A single slice index means from there to the end.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving strings — split join.
questions.explanation: split turns '295' into 3 characters and join inserts a dash between each pair, giving 5 characters. There are one fewer separators than digits. Carrying the operation through gives 5; common slips include ignoring the inserted separators and counting a separator after the last digit.
questions.hint: Count the dashes between digits, not after the last one.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving objects — access.

stimulus.body: A program is processing the value 296.

options.misconception: Assuming a missing key yields zero

questions.explanation: Bracket access with the exact key string retrieves 296, and adding one gives 297. A mistyped key would produce undefined, not zero. The printed value is 297, while the alternatives come from forgetting the addition of one, adding two by mistake and assuming a missing key yields zero.
questions.hint: Bracket notation uses the key name as a string.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving objects — keys.

options.misconception: Assuming only the first property is enumerable
Counting entries as if values were keys

questions.explanation: Object.keys returns the enumerable own property names, which are a, b and c, so its length is three. Values such as 297 do not affect the count. The printed value is 3, while the alternatives come from counting only numeric-looking keys, counting entries as if values were keys and assuming only the first property is enumerable.
questions.hint: keys returns names, not the stored values.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving objects — destructuring.
questions.explanation: Destructuring binds a to 298 and b to 2 by matching property names, so their sum is 300. Order in the pattern does not matter for objects. Carrying the operation through gives 300; common slips include using only the first destructured field and using only the second field.
questions.hint: Object destructuring matches by property name.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — spread.

options.misconception: Assuming the spread discards the extra value
Counting the spread as adding two values

questions.explanation: The spread expands the two existing entries and the trailing value is appended, giving 3 elements. The spread form creates a fresh array rather than mutating arr. The printed value is 3, while the alternatives come from assuming the spread discards the extra value, counting the spread as adding two values and reporting only the appended element.
questions.hint: Spread copies existing items before the new one is added.
